288.title: Named in Congress (2015)
288.hook: Pope Francis names Merton among four great Americans
288.howItsDone: Catholics remember holy men and women in the Church's calendar of saints and in prayers for the dead, and many honor teachers like Merton and Dorothy Day by reading their work and continuing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bangkok: Merton's death, twenty-seven years to the day after he entered the monastery. Your line was the day he began. Who did you remember? Today, nearly fifty years later, he's remembered somewhere very loud. Day two hundred eighty-eight.

The United States Capitol, September 24, 2015. The chamber of the House of Representatives is packed: senators, representatives, justices, cameras. For the first time in history, a pope stands at the podium to address Congress. Pope Francis speaks in English, slowly, about immigrants, the poor, the death penalty, and the earth. And to hold it all together, he tells the story of four Americans. Three are a president, a preacher and a journalist who fed the hungry. The fourth is a monk who'd spent most of his adult life in silence. Today: named in Congress.
screen: `THE CAPITOL, SEPTEMBER 24, 2015.` → `A POPE ADDRESSES CONGRESS.` → `FOUR AMERICANS.`

segments.voice: First, the four. Pope Francis named Abraham Lincoln, for liberty. Martin Luther King Jr., for his dream of rights for all. Dorothy Day, the Catholic journalist who co-founded the Catholic Worker and spent her life serving the poor. And Thomas Merton. Second, what he said about Merton. Francis called him a man of dialogue and a promoter of peace between peoples and religions. Above all, he said, Merton was a man of prayer, a thinker who challenged the certainties of his time and opened new horizons for souls and for the Church. Look at that list: prayer, dialogue, peace, challenge. It's every stretch of the road we've walked these weeks. Third, why it was a surprise. For years, some Catholics had been uneasy about Merton: his outspokenness about war, his friendships across traditions, his restless questions. To hear a pope name him in front of Congress, beside Lincoln and King, told his readers that his questions had a home in the Church. Fourth, remembering as a Catholic act. At the Last Supper, Jesus said, in the Douay-Rheims: "Do this for a commemoration of me." Catholics believe remembering isn't just nostalgia. It keeps a person's gift alive and working in the present. The Church remembers its saints on their feast days. Merton isn't a canonized saint, but a pope chose to remember him out loud. A monk who ran from fame was held up for a whole nation, because of what his hidden life had given.
screen: `LINCOLN, KING, DAY, MERTON.` · `A MAN OF DIALOGUE AND PRAYER.` · `HIS QUESTIONS HAD A HOME.` · `REMEMBERING KEEPS A GIFT ALIVE.` · then, large: `DO THIS FOR A COMMEMORATION OF ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name someone who shaped you. Look around for one thing that carries a person in it: a song you hum, a phrase you repeat, a book on the shelf, the way you fold a shirt. Follow it back to whoever gave it to you: a grandparent, a teacher, a coach, an author you never met. Say their name quietly, once. Then name the gift in a few words, and stay grateful for a moment. If you pray, you can thank God for them, living or dead. The bell holds the time.
Named in Congress. In 2015, Pope Francis held Merton up beside Lincoln, King and Dorothy Day, as a man of prayer, dialogue and peace. Today's word.
Your line: a monk remembered. Today, tell someone about a person who shaped you. Say their name out loud, and keep their gift working. Day two hundred eighty-eight.

the Catholic Worker and the poor

289.title: What Merton gives
289.hook: holiness is becoming who you truly are before God
289.howItsDone: Catholics believe every person is called to holiness, a teaching the Second Vatican Council called the universal call to holiness, and many read Merton, the saints and scripture to discover their own particular path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, named in Congress: a pope holding up a hidden monk before a nation. Your line was a monk remembered. Whose name did you say out loud? Today we close our eighteen days with Merton. Day two hundred eighty-nine.

When people hear the word saint, they often picture someone who isn't quite human. A statue with a halo and a blank, faraway look. Perfect, and a little boring. And they think: well, that's not me. I'm too messy, too loud, too ordinary. Thomas Merton had a very different picture. After all the restlessness, the monastery, the books, the woods and the long trip east, he left one idea that people keep coming back to. Holiness isn't becoming someone else. Today: what Merton gives.
screen: `A STATUE WITH A FARAWAY LOOK.` → `THAT'S NOT ME.` → `NOT BECOMING SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: First, the idea. In New Seeds of Contemplation, Merton wrote that for him, to be a saint means to be himself. Not a copy of someone else's holiness. The real person God had in mind. He said a tree gives glory to God by being a tree, fully, and not trying to be something else. Second, the root. This isn't self-help. For Merton, your true self isn't something you invent. It's who God knows you to be. The prophet Jeremiah hears God say, in the Douay-Rheims: "Before I formed thee in the bowels of thy mother, I knew thee." In that line, the prophet is known before he has done anything. For Merton, holiness is growing into being known like that, the way a seed grows into the tree it already is. Third, the road we've walked. Look back at these eighteen days. A restless young man, orphaned and drifting. A convert drawn in New York. A Trappist in the silence. A mountain climbed one ledge at a time. Vigils before dawn. Waking up. The false self and the true. Seeds everywhere. Strangers shining on a street corner. Not knowing the road. A hermit in the woods. A monk speaking about war and race, making friends across traditions, alone for others. A clear morning in Sri Lanka, and a sudden end in Bangkok. That's not a perfect life. It's a real one, becoming itself before God. Fourth, what he gives. Merton gives permission. Permission to be restless, to ask questions, to not know, to love people who differ from you, to keep changing. And, underneath, his conviction that the person God made you to be is worth becoming.
screen: `TO BE A SAINT IS TO BE MYSELF.` · `KNOWN BEFORE YOU WERE FORMED.` · `EIGHTEEN DAYS, ONE REAL LIFE.` · `PERMISSION TO BECOME.` · then, large: `BEFORE I FORMED THEE, I KNEW THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be yourself on purpose. Sit easy, and breathe. Think of one thing that's truly you, a way you laugh, a thing you love, a kind of kindness only you seem to do. Not the polished version. The real one. Let yourself be glad of it for a moment, without comparing it to anyone. Then imagine offering it back, as a gift that was always meant to be given. If you pray, you can thank God for making you you. The bell holds the time.
What Merton gives. His lasting idea: holiness is becoming who you truly are before God, a road he believed anyone could walk. Today's word.

Your line: become who you are. Today, do one thing that is truly you, on purpose, without apologizing. That closes our days with Merton. Tomorrow we open the map of the Catholic faith. Day two hundred eighty-nine.

screen: `DAY 289 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A MAP, NOT A WALL.`

290.title: A map, not a wall
290.hook: four pillars: what we believe, how we celebrate, how we live, how we pray
290.howItsDone: Catholics use the Catechism of the Catholic Church as a reference for teaching the faith, and parishes build their classes for children, teens and adults joining the Church around its four parts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what Merton gives: holiness as becoming who you are before God. Your line was become who you are. What did you do on purpose? Today, a new part of the path, and a big book. Day two hundred ninety.

On a shelf in a parish office sits a thick book. Not the Bible, the other one. Heavy, a little intimidating, full of numbered paragraphs. Sometimes there's one on a relative's nightstand with a rosary on top. From the outside it can look like a list of rules, a wall: everything you can't do. Open it, though, and it's built more like a map, with roads that connect. Today: the catechism.
screen: `THE OTHER BIG BOOK ON THE SHELF.` → `A LIST OF RULES?` → `BUILT MORE LIKE A MAP.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Catechism comes from a Greek verb, katechein, built on the word for sound, as in echo. It means to teach by word of mouth, to make something resound in someone's ear. Luke uses it at the start of his Gospel, telling a man named Theophilus he writes so that, in the Douay-Rheims, "thou mayest know the verity of those words in which thou hast been instructed." Instructed there is that echo word. The faith was passed on out loud long before it was printed. Second, the book. There have been many catechisms. After the Council of Trent came the Roman Catechism in 1566. In the United States, the Baltimore Catechism of 1885 taught by question and answer: Why did God make you? To know him, to love him, and to serve him in this world, and to be happy with him forever in the next. In 1992, Pope John Paul II released the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the one on shelves today: two thousand eight hundred sixty-five numbered paragraphs. Third, the four pillars. It's built in four parts. What Catholics believe: the Creed. How they celebrate: the liturgy and the seven sacraments. How they live: life in Christ, the commandments and the virtues. And how they pray: ending with the Our Father. Belief, worship, life, prayer. Fourth, why a map. The Catechism isn't meant to be read cover to cover like a rulebook. It's meant to show how everything connects: why a belief shapes a sacrament, why a sacrament shapes a life, why a life turns into prayer. For the next weeks, we'll walk it, one theme at a time.
screen: `KATECHEIN — TO MAKE IT ECHO.` · `TRENT, BALTIMORE, THEN 1992.` · `BELIEVE, CELEBRATE, LIVE, PRAY.` · `EVERYTHING CONNECTS.` · then, large: `FOUR PILLARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand among the four pillars. Breathe out slowly. Picture four stone columns holding up a roof. Touch the first: what you believe, or wonder about. The second: how you celebrate, a Mass, a feast, a candle. The third: how you live, one choice today. The fourth: how you pray, or how you'd like to. Notice which pillar feels strongest in your life right now, and which feels thin. No judgment. Just notice. If you pray, you can ask for help with the thin one. The bell holds the time.
Catechism. From the Greek for making something echo: a summary of the faith, taught aloud and passed on. Today's Catechism has four pillars. Today's word.
Your line: four pillars. Today, if you can, look up the Catechism's table of contents online and just read the four part titles. Believe, celebrate, live, pray. Day two hundred ninety.

291.title: The desire for God (CCC 27)
291.hook: the longing for God is written in every heart
291.howItsDone: The Catechism of the Catholic Church opens its account of the faith with the human desire for God (paragraphs 27–30), and quotes Augustine's line about the restless heart (paragraph 30).

segments.voice: Yesterday, the catechism: a map of the faith, not a wall. Your line was four pillars. Believe, celebrate, live, pray. Today we open the first page of the first pillar. Day two hundred ninety-one.

A woman gets the job she worked toward for years. The offer letter, the new desk, the dinner to celebrate. And it's good. It really is. But a few weeks in, something small shows up, like hunger after a big meal: is this it? She wonders if she's ungrateful. She wonders if something's broken in her. She doesn't tell anyone. The first chapter of the Catechism of the Catholic Church doesn't start with rules. It starts with that ache. Today: the desire for God.
screen: `SHE GETS THE THING SHE WANTED.` → `IS THIS IT?` → `CHAPTER ONE STARTS WITH THE ACHE.`

segments.voice: First, where it begins. Paragraph 27, the start of the Catechism's first chapter, says the desire for God is written in the human heart, because people are made by God and for God. And it says God never stops drawing people toward himself. Only in God, it says, will a person find the truth and happiness they never stop looking for. So, in the Catechism's view, that ache after the good thing isn't a defect. It's a signature. Second, the oldest voice. A few paragraphs on, the Catechism quotes Augustine, from the opening of his Confessions, in a line addressed to God. In Pusey's translation: "for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." You heard its echo in young Merton's restlessness. Here it becomes the foundation of the whole book. Third, everywhere. The Catechism notes that, throughout history, people have searched for God in prayers, sacrifices, rituals and quiet meditation. It calls the human being a religious being. It doesn't treat that search as a problem, but as a trace of the desire. It also admits honestly that people can forget this longing, or push it away, or never think about it. Fourth, the psalm. Long before Augustine, a psalm put it in one picture, in the Douay-Rheims: "As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God." A deer at a stream, thirsty. Catholics say that thirst isn't the problem. It's the clue: a sign of being made for more.
screen: `WRITTEN IN THE HUMAN HEART.` · `RESTLESS UNTIL IT REPOSE IN THEE.` · `A RELIGIOUS BEING, EVERYWHERE.` · `THE THIRSTY DEER.` · then, large: `SO MY SOUL PANTETH AFTER THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what you long for most. Settle and breathe. Ask yourself, honestly: what do I want? Let the first answers come: money, rest, love, to be understood. Don't judge them. Then ask again, underneath: and what do I want from that? Keep going gently, one layer at a time, until you reach something you can't quite name. Stay there. If you pray, you can offer that longing to God, just as it is. The bell holds the time.
The desire for God. The first thing the Catechism's first chapter says about people: a longing written in the human heart, because, it says, they're made by God and for God. Today's word.
Your line: made for more. Today, if that little is-this-it ache shows up, don't scold it or scroll it away. Treat it as a clue. Day two hundred ninety-one.

292.title: Faith and reason (CCC 159)
292.hook: truth can't contradict truth; faith and reason are two wings
292.howItsDone: Catholic schools and universities teach science alongside theology, the Vatican runs an astronomical observatory, and the Pontifical Academy of Sciences brings together scientists of many faiths and none.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the desire for God, written in every heart. Your line was made for more. Did you catch the ache and treat it as a clue? Today, what happens when that longing meets a microscope. Day two hundred ninety-two.

There's a story a lot of people absorb without anyone telling it to them directly: you have to pick. Science or faith. Reason or religion. Smart people in labs, pious people in pews, and never the two shall meet. Then you learn that the man who first proposed what we now call the Big Bang was a Belgian Catholic priest. That the father of genetics was a friar growing peas in a monastery garden. And that the Vatican runs an astronomical observatory. Maybe the story is wrong. Today: faith and reason.
screen: `SCIENCE OR FAITH: PICK ONE?` → `A PRIEST AND THE BIG BANG.` → `A FRIAR AND HIS PEAS.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. Paragraph 159 of the Catechism says that although faith goes beyond reason, there can never be a real conflict between them. Why? Because the same God who reveals the mysteries of faith also gave human beings the light of reason, and God can't contradict himself. It borrows a line from the First Vatican Council: truth can't contradict truth. And it adds that honest scientific research, done well and ethically, will never truly conflict with faith, because the things of the world and the things of faith come from the same God. Second, the old root. Paul says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." To study creation carefully is, for Catholics, one way of reading God's handwriting. Third, the people. Georges Lemaître, a priest and physicist, proposed in the 1920s and 30s that the universe began from a single primeval atom. Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, worked out the basic laws of heredity. And honesty matters here: the Church also got it badly wrong with Galileo, condemning him in 1633. In 1992, Pope John Paul II publicly acknowledged the errors of the theologians who judged him. Fourth, the two wings. In 1998, John Paul II wrote a letter called Faith and Reason. It opens with an image: faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises toward the truth. A bird with one wing just goes in circles. Catholics are asked to fly with both.
screen: `TRUTH CAN'T CONTRADICT TRUTH.` · `READ BY THE THINGS THAT ARE MADE.` · `LEMAÎTRE, MENDEL, AND GALILEO.` · `TWO WINGS.` · then, large: `THE INVISIBLE THINGS OF HIM ARE CLEARLY SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wonder with both wings. Settle and breathe. Think of one thing science has taught you that still amazes you. The light from some stars left them before humans existed. Your body replaces most of its cells over time. There are more cells in you than stars in our galaxy. Pick one and let it sink in. Don't rush to a lesson. Just be amazed. If you pray, you can let the wonder turn into thanks. The bell holds the time.
Faith and reason. The Catholic conviction that they can't truly contradict each other, because both come from the same God. Two wings. Today's word.
Your line: two wings. Today, learn one new science fact, from a video, an article, a kid's question, and let it make you wonder. Day two hundred ninety-two.

293.title: Scripture and Tradition (CCC 80–83)
293.hook: Catholics receive God's word through both the Bible and the living handing-on
293.howItsDone: Catholics receive Scripture and Tradition together, especially in the liturgy, where the Bible is read and the ancient creeds and prayers are handed on from generation to generation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith and reason: two wings that can't truly contradict each other. Your line was two wings. What made you wonder? Today, how the faith reached you in the first place. Day two hundred ninety-three.

A stained index card in a kitchen drawer: Grandma's recipe, in her handwriting. But the card never tells you everything. How thick the batter should look. When to turn the heat down. The little thing she did with the spoon. You learned that by standing next to her in the kitchen. The card and the kitchen go together; lose either one, and the dish isn't quite right. Catholics say God's word reached them something like that. Today: Scripture and Tradition.
screen: `GRANDMA'S RECIPE CARD.` → `WHAT THE CARD DOESN'T SAY.` → `THE CARD AND THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Tradition comes from the Latin tradere, to hand over. It's a word about passing something from one pair of hands to the next. Paul uses the idea about the Last Supper, in the Douay-Rheims: "For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you." Received, delivered. Handed on. Second, before the book. The apostles preached before any of the New Testament was written down. And John's Gospel ends by admitting it couldn't hold everything: Jesus did many other things, and if they were all written, the world itself couldn't contain the books. So Catholics say the faith was passed on two ways from the start: in writing, and in the living life of the Church, its preaching, worship, and practice. Paul tells the Thessalonians to "hold the traditions which you have learned, whether by word, or by our epistle." Third, one source. The Catechism, in paragraphs 80 to 83, says Scripture and Tradition flow from the same divine wellspring and work together, like two streams from one spring. It also draws a careful line. Capital-T Tradition is the faith handed down from the apostles. Small-t traditions, like local customs and particular devotions, can change over time. Fourth, who says what. Orthodox Christians also hold Scripture and Holy Tradition together. Many Protestant churches teach that Scripture alone is the final authority, while still valuing the creeds and the early Church. Catholics hold both, the card and the kitchen, and believe the faith came to them through real hands, all the way back.
screen: `TRADERE — TO HAND OVER.` · `PREACHED BEFORE IT WAS WRITTEN.` · `ONE WELLSPRING, TWO STREAMS.` · `THE CARD AND THE KITCHEN.` · then, large: `THAT WHICH ALSO I DELIVERED UNTO YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trace the hands. Settle in. Ask: who handed faith, or the question of God, to me? A parent teaching you to pray. A teacher. A friend who brought you to church. A book, a stranger. Picture that person's hands. Then think of who handed it to them, and to them, back and back, a long chain of hands. You're one link. If you pray, you can thank God for each one you can name. The bell holds the time.
Tradition. From the Latin for handing over: the faith passed down from the apostles in the living life of the Church, together with Scripture. Today's word.
Your line: handed on. Today, ask one person who handed their faith, or their values, to them. Then listen to the story. Day two hundred ninety-three.

the faith was passed on by word and life before it was written down.

fork.reveal: "hold the traditions which you have learned, whether by word, or by our epistle": both the spoken and the written.

trapdoor: what you thought: tradition means old customs.
what it means: the faith handed on from the apostles, living alongside Scripture, as the card goes with the kitchen.
what a scholar hears: tradere, the same root as traitor, the traditores who handed over sacred books in persecution; Dei Verbum 9; and the T/t distinction of CCC 83.

sources.ref: Catechism of the Catholic Church 80–83; Dei Verbum 9

294.title: The teaching office (CCC 85–87)
294.hook: the pope and bishops serve the word of God, not above it
294.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the pope and their local bishop by name in every Mass, in the Eucharistic Prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tradition: the faith handed on, the card and the kitchen together. Your line was handed on. Whose story did you hear? Today: who makes sure the recipe doesn't drift. Day two hundred ninety-four.

Play a game of telephone with twenty people and see what comes out the other end. A sentence about a purple cat turns into something about a pirate's hat. Every person meant well. It drifted anyway. Now try passing on a message for two thousand years, through language after language. Catholics believe God didn't leave that to chance. So who gets to say what it means? And what keeps them honest? Today: the teaching office.
screen: `A GAME OF TELEPHONE.` → `TWO THOUSAND YEARS OF PASSING IT ON.` → `WHO KEEPS IT FROM DRIFTING?`

segments.voice: First, the name. Magisterium comes from the Latin magister, teacher. It's the Church's teaching office: the bishops, together with the pope, the bishop of Rome. Catholics believe Christ gave the apostles the task of teaching, and that it passed to their successors. In Luke, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells the disciples he sends out: "He that heareth you, heareth me." Second, the surprise. Some people expect the Catechism to put the teaching office above the Bible. It says the opposite. Paragraph 86, borrowing from the Second Vatican Council, says the Magisterium is not above the word of God, but is its servant. It teaches only what has been handed on. It listens to the word devotedly, guards it, and explains it faithfully. The pope and bishops are meant to be servants of the word, not its owners. Third, the old title. Since at least the time of Pope Gregory the Great, about the year 600, popes have signed documents with the title servant of the servants of God. It's still used today. Fourth, what it isn't. A common myth says Catholics believe the pope can't be wrong about anything. Not so. The Church teaches that the pope is protected from error only under strict conditions, when he solemnly defines a matter of faith or morals for the whole Church. That's been used very rarely. Most of the time, the teaching office does what the word says: it teaches, and it serves, so the faith doesn't drift in the telephone game of history.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold up the servants. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind the pope, and the bishop where you live, if you know his name. Whatever you think of them, picture them as tired human beings with a heavy job: to serve a word bigger than themselves. If you pray, you can pray for them, that they listen well and serve faithfully. If you don't pray, you can simply wish them wisdom. The bell holds the time.
Magisterium. From the Latin for teacher: the Church's teaching office, the pope and bishops, serving the word of God rather than standing above it. Today's word.
